messages.content: You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do I make more flytraps?

You have three routes: leaf pullings, dividing a mature clump, or seed. Leaf pullings are the quickest and most reliable - pull an outer leaf downward so it comes away with a bit of the white rhizome base attached, lay it flat on damp peat and perlite mix, and keep it bright and humid until plantlets show in about 4 to 8 weeks. Clumps that have grown several crowns can be split in early spring. Seed works too, but it takes 3 to 5 years to get an adult-sized plant, so most people start with pullings.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Can I just cut a leaf off and stick it in the dirt?

Cutting will not work for a Venus flytrap - a leaf snipped off partway up the petiole has no meristem tissue and simply rots. What you want is a pulling: grip the base of an outer leaf and tug gently downward and outward so it peels off the rhizome with a small piece of the white base still attached. That white base is the essential part, and without it the leaf will never strike. Lay it on damp mix rather than burying it, and keep it humid.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Step by step, how do I take a Venus flytrap leaf pulling?

Start with a healthy plant and pick an outer leaf from the perimeter of the rosette. Hold it right at the soil line and pull downward and slightly sideways so it separates cleanly, taking a sliver of the white rhizome base with it. Lay the whole leaf flat on damp peat and perlite mix, trap and all, press the white base into light contact with the surface, and cover the container or bag it to hold humidity in bright light. Plantlets usually appear at the white base in about 4 to 8 weeks, and you can pot them individually once they have a few of their own leaves.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
My flytrap pulling has been sitting there for two months and nothing has happened. What went wrong?

The most common cause is that the pulling came away without any of the white rhizome base - a bare green leaf has nothing to grow from and will just yellow off. Check the end of the leaf; if it is a clean green break rather than a pale swollen bit of tissue, that is your answer. The other usual culprits are low light or letting the mix dry out. Given good conditions and an intact white base, plantlets show in roughly 4 to 8 weeks, so at two months with nothing it is worth starting over with a fresh pulling.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
how many pullings can i take at once without killing the plant

On a healthy adult flytrap, taking two or three outer leaves is fine and the plant will replace them over the growing season. Stripping a plant bare stresses it badly and can set it back a full year, so leave the majority of the rosette intact. If you want a lot of pullings, take a few, let the plant recover for six to eight weeks, then take a few more. Never take pullings from a plant that is already weak or newly repotted.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
When is the right time to split a flytrap that has turned into a clump?

Early spring, just as the plant is waking from dormancy, is the ideal window - the plant has a whole season ahead to re-root. Knock it out of the pot, wash the peat off the rhizomes so you can see where the individual crowns join, and tease or cut them apart so each division has its own white rhizome and some roots. Pot each piece in fresh 1:1 peat and perlite, water it in with distilled water, and expect a few weeks of sulking before new growth appears.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How long does it take to grow a Venus flytrap from seed?

Germination takes roughly 4 to 6 weeks after sowing and can be uneven, with stragglers coming up over a couple of months. The seedlings are tiny - traps barely a millimetre or two across in the first year - and it takes 3 to 5 years to reach adult size. That long wait is why most growers buy divisions or take leaf pullings when they just want more plants. Seed is worth it if you are after genetic variation or want to select new forms.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Do flytrap seeds need to go in the fridge first?

Yes, flytrap seed is from a temperate species and germinates far better after cold stratification. Put the seed in a small bag of damp sphagnum or between damp paper towels and keep it in the fridge for several weeks before sowing. After that, sow it on the surface of damp peat mix, keep it warm, humid and brightly lit, and expect germination in about 4 to 6 weeks. Do not bury the seed - it needs light on the surface.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Should I let my flytrap flower if I want seed?

You can, but be aware that flowering costs a flytrap a lot of energy and a plant that sets seed often grows noticeably weaker for the rest of the season. If you want seed, let the stalk run on a strong mature plant, hand pollinate the open flowers with a small brush, and collect the shiny black seed a few weeks later when the pods dry and split. On smaller or newly potted plants, cut the stalk off at the base as soon as you see it. Remember the resulting seedlings need 3 to 5 years to reach full size.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do you divide a Sarracenia?

Early spring, right at the end of dormancy, is the time to do it. Lift the plant out of its pot and rinse enough media off to expose the thick horizontal rhizome, then cut it into sections with a clean sharp knife, making sure every section has its own roots and at least one growth point. Pot the divisions in fresh 1:1 peat and sand or perlite at the same depth they were growing, and water them in with distilled water. Small divisions may skip pitchers for a season while they re-establish.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
my pitcher plant has outgrown its pot and has like four growing points, what now

That is a plant ready to divide. Wait for early spring, tip it out, wash the rhizome clean and cut it into pieces so each one carries at least one growth point and a decent share of roots. Four growth points could give you three or four plants, though larger divisions establish faster than tiny ones. Fresh nutrient-free mix and a pot with room for a couple of years of rhizome growth will set them up nicely.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do I germinate Sarracenia seed?

Sarracenia is temperate, so the seed needs several weeks of cold stratification first - damp sphagnum or damp paper towel in a sealed bag in the fridge. Then sow it on the surface of damp peat and sand without covering it, keep it warm, bright and humid, and wait roughly 4 to 6 weeks for germination, which is often staggered. Seedlings are slow, taking around 3 to 5 years to reach flowering size. Keep them in the same nutrient-free conditions as adults, just with more consistent humidity in the first year.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Is there a way to stratify seed without a fridge?

If you live somewhere with real winters, sowing the seed on the surface of damp mix in autumn and leaving the pot outdoors gives the same effect - several weeks of cold and damp followed by natural spring warmth. Just protect the pot from heavy rain washing the seed away and from birds. The fridge method is more controlled and lets you time germination, but the outdoor route works fine for temperate species like Sarracenia, flytraps and temperate sundews. Tropical species need no cold at all and should just be sown warm.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How long do I leave seed in the fridge?

Several weeks is the standard, and four to six weeks in damp sphagnum or on damp paper in a sealed bag suits Venus flytrap, Sarracenia and temperate sundew seed well. Longer does not hurt much, but the seed must stay damp and must not freeze solid or dry out. Check the bag every week or two for mould and discard anything furry. Once out of the fridge, sow on the surface and provide warmth, humidity and bright light.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Which carnivorous plant seeds do NOT need cold treatment?

Tropical and subtropical species skip stratification entirely - Nepenthes, tropical sundews like Drosera capensis and Drosera spatulata, tropical butterworts and most Mexican Pinguicula. Sow those straight onto the surface of damp mix, keep them warm and humid, and they will come up in a few weeks. Cold treatment is only needed for temperate species that experience real winters, meaning Venus flytraps, Sarracenia and temperate sundews. Giving tropical seed a fridge spell does not usually help and can just waste time.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Do I bury carnivorous plant seed or not?

Sow it on the surface and leave it uncovered. Most carnivorous plant seed is tiny and needs light to germinate, so burying it under even a thin layer of mix will stop it. Scatter it evenly over damp mix, press it very lightly so it makes contact, then cover the pot with a lid or bag to hold humidity. Keep it warm and brightly lit and expect the first seedlings in about 4 to 6 weeks.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How long until seed comes up?

Plan on around 4 to 6 weeks for most carnivorous plant seed once it has been sown warm, humid and in good light. Germination is often erratic, so do not throw a pot away after the first flush - stragglers can appear for two or three months afterwards. Temperate species that were not properly stratified may not come up at all, or may trickle up unevenly. Keep the surface damp with distilled water throughout and resist the urge to disturb the pot.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What do I do with carnivorous seedlings once they sprout?

Keep them exactly as they were during germination for the first few months: surface damp, high humidity under a lid or bag, and bright light, ideally a strong lamp close overhead or gentle direct sun. Ventilate a little more each week from around three months so they gradually acclimatise to open air rather than collapsing when uncovered suddenly. Do not fertilize, do not prick them out too early, and use only distilled or rainwater. They will start catching their own tiny prey when they are ready.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
When can I move seedlings into their own pots?

Wait until they are big enough to handle without crushing, which is usually somewhere between six months and a year for flytraps and Sarracenia, less for fast sundews. Lift a clump with a plastic label or toothpick rather than pulling on the leaves, keep as much mix around the roots as you can, and settle each one into fresh 1:1 peat and perlite. Water in with distilled water and keep them covered and humid for a couple of weeks while they settle. Many growers leave seedlings as a communal tray for the first year, which is perfectly fine.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Why does it take so long to grow these from seed?

Carnivorous plants grow in nutrient-poor bogs where the whole strategy is slow, steady accumulation rather than fast growth, and their seedlings start extremely small - a first-year flytrap trap is a couple of millimetres wide. They also spend energy building traps and, in temperate species, lose several months a year to dormancy. Add that up and it takes 3 to 5 years to get from seed to a full-sized flytrap or a flowering Sarracenia. Vegetative propagation shortcuts all of that, which is why leaf pullings and divisions are the normal way to bulk up a collection.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do I propagate a sundew from a leaf?

Cut a healthy, actively growing leaf near its base and either lay it dewy side up on damp sphagnum or float it on a shallow dish of distilled water. Put it in a covered container in bright light, and plantlets will form along the leaf within a few weeks. Once each plantlet has a few of its own leaves and visible roots, pot it into 1:1 peat and sand and keep it humid while it settles. This works especially well on Drosera capensis, binata and spatulata.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
does floating a sundew leaf in water actually work

It does, and it is one of the easiest propagation tricks there is. Use distilled or rainwater in a small covered pot or takeaway tub, float the cut leaf on the surface, and set it somewhere bright but not baking. Little green plantlets appear along the leaf within a few weeks, and once they have roots you move them onto damp peat and sand. The container needs to be covered so humidity stays high and the leaf does not simply dry up.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What are root cuttings and which sundews are they good for?

A root cutting is a length of thick root laid on damp media that then sprouts a whole new plant from the root tissue itself. It suits sundews with fleshy, substantial roots - Drosera capensis, binata and regia are classic candidates - and is a handy way to get plants from something you have just repotted. Cut healthy root sections a couple of centimetres long, lay them on damp sphagnum or peat, cover for humidity and keep them bright. New shoots typically break the surface within a few weeks.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
My cape sundew is popping up everywhere in my other pots. Is that normal?

Completely normal - Drosera capensis is a prolific self-seeder and will colonise every pot in the tray if you let it. The flowers self-pollinate without any help, and each stalk throws out huge numbers of fine seeds that germinate wherever the mix stays damp. If you want to stop it, snip the flower stalks off before the pods dry and split. Otherwise, enjoy the free plants and pot up the seedlings once they are big enough to handle - they are excellent for giving away.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do I take a cutting from a Nepenthes vine?

Choose a section of vine with two or three nodes on it and cut just below the bottom node with a clean blade. Strip the lower leaves off, cut the remaining leaves in half across to cut water loss, then insert the base into damp long fibre sphagnum. Keep the cutting in very high humidity - a sealed bag, propagator or tank - with bright indirect light and warmth, and roots should form in about 1 to 3 months. Do not tug at it to check; wait for new growth from a node as the sign that it has rooted.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Should I use rooting hormone on Nepenthes cuttings?

Rooting hormone is optional but does tend to improve the strike rate and speed things up a little. Dust or dip the cut end lightly before pushing it into damp sphagnum, and do not overdo it - a thin coating is plenty. What matters much more is the basics: two or three nodes, lower leaves removed, remaining leaves cut in half, and consistently high humidity. Expect roots in about 1 to 3 months either way.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How humid does it need to be for Nepenthes cuttings to root?

Essentially saturated - the cutting has no roots and can only survive if it barely loses any water, so aim for near 100 percent humidity. A sealed clear bag around the pot, a lidded propagator or a small tank all work well. Give it warm temperatures and bright indirect light, never direct sun through the plastic, and open it briefly every few days for fresh air. Once new growth appears after roughly 1 to 3 months, start venting gradually over several weeks to harden it off.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
My Nepenthes cutting has been in sphagnum for six weeks with no roots. Should I bin it?

Not yet - rooting commonly takes 1 to 3 months, so six weeks is well inside the normal range. As long as the stem is still firm and green and the leaf halves have not gone black, it is still in the game. Check that the humidity is genuinely high and that the sphagnum is damp but not waterlogged, since a sodden mix rots the base. Give it another month or two before making a decision.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What is a basal shoot on a Nepenthes and can I remove it?

A basal shoot is a new growth point that breaks from the base of the plant, usually once the main stem has started to vine. You can separate it, but only once it has developed its own roots - cut it away from the parent with a clean blade, keeping those roots intact, and pot it into an airy sphagnum and bark mix. Keep it in high humidity for a few weeks while it settles in. If it has no roots of its own yet, treat it as a cutting instead and root it in damp sphagnum.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do you propagate a butterwort?

Leaf pullings are the standard method and they are easiest during the succulent winter phase, when Mexican butterworts produce small plump non-carnivorous leaves. Detach one of those leaves with a gentle sideways pull so the entire base comes away cleanly, then lay it on damp sand or peat mix in bright light. Little plantlets form at the base over the following weeks and can be potted on once they have roots. Butterworts also make offsets around the parent, which you can separate at repotting time.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Why do butterwort pullings work better in winter?

In the winter succulent phase the leaves are thick, firm and full of stored reserves, so they come away cleanly with their whole base and can support a new plantlet. Summer carnivorous leaves are thin, sticky and floppy, and they tend to tear or rot before anything forms. Pull a plump winter leaf sideways so the base separates intact, lay it on damp sand or peat mix in bright light, and be patient. The key is the same as with flytraps - if the base does not come with the leaf, it will not strike.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How often should I repot my carnivorous plants?

Every 1 to 2 years for most of them. Sphagnum peat breaks down and compacts over time, which suffocates roots and lets minerals build up, so refreshing the mix matters even when the plant looks happy in its pot. Early spring at the end of dormancy is the ideal time for temperate species, and tropicals like Nepenthes can go any time they are actively growing. Always use fresh nutrient-free mix and never fertilizer, potting soil or compost.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Whats the best time of year to repot a flytrap?

Early spring, right at the end of dormancy, when the plant is about to push new growth and can re-root quickly. That timing also lets you divide any extra crowns at the same time. Repotting in the middle of summer is possible in an emergency but the plant will sulk harder and may drop a few traps. Avoid disturbing the roots in autumn, when the plant is winding down and has no time to recover before dormancy.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Is it ever OK to repot outside of spring?

Yes, if there is a real reason - the plant arrived bare root, the mix has gone sour or mouldy, or it is drowning in a broken-down peat sludge. In those cases repot straight away rather than waiting, since bad media does more damage than the disturbance. Just expect a slower recovery and keep the plant a little shadier and more humid than usual for the first couple of weeks. For routine refreshes, early spring is still the best window.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do I repot without wrecking the roots?

Water the plant first so the rootball holds together, then squeeze the pot and slide the plant out rather than pulling it by the leaves. Support the rootball in one hand, and if you need to clear old peat away, tease it off gently with your fingers or rinse it with distilled water instead of scraping. Sarracenia and flytrap roots are brittle, so accept that you will break a few - it is not fatal. Settle the plant at its original depth in fresh mix, firm lightly, and water thoroughly with distilled water.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What soil mix should I use when I repot?

For most carnivorous plants, a 1:1 blend of sphagnum peat and perlite or silica sand is the standard - cheap, reliable and completely nutrient free. Nepenthes want something much airier, so use long fibre sphagnum with bark chips and perlite so the roots get plenty of oxygen. Rinse perlite and sand before mixing to remove dust and any mineral residue, and dampen the mix with distilled water before potting. Never add fertilizer, potting soil, compost or anything sold as enriched.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Can I reuse the old peat when I repot?

Better not to. The whole point of repotting every 1 to 2 years is that old peat has broken down, compacted and accumulated minerals from watering and from decaying roots. Reusing it puts the plant straight back into the problem you were solving. Mix a fresh batch of 1:1 peat and perlite or sand, dampen it with distilled water, and put the old material on the garden instead.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What size pot should I use?

Go deeper rather than wider for most species - flytraps and Sarracenia send roots well down, so a pot 12 to 15 cm deep suits a flytrap and 20 cm or more suits a mature Sarracenia. Allow a bit of width for a couple of years of rhizome spread but avoid a huge pot around a small plant, since a big volume of soggy mix stays wet and sour. Nepenthes are shallow rooted and prefer wider, shallower pots or baskets. Use plastic or glazed ceramic, never terracotta, because unglazed clay leaches minerals into the mix.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Why cant I use terracotta pots?

Unglazed terracotta contains minerals and salts that leach into the media, and carnivorous plants are adapted to essentially mineral-free conditions, so it slowly poisons them. The porous walls also wick moisture out fast, which fights the constantly damp conditions bog plants need. Plastic pots or glazed ceramic are the correct choice and cost less anyway. If you love the look of clay, drop a plastic pot inside a terracotta cachepot so nothing touches the mix.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Do I water differently right after repotting?

Water thoroughly with distilled or rainwater immediately after potting to settle the mix around the roots and drive out air pockets. After that, keep the media damp as usual - a shallow tray of distilled water works well for flytraps and Sarracenia. Do not add fertilizer or any kind of tonic, ever. Keep the plant in slightly gentler light for the first week or so while the damaged roots recover.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
My plant looks awful since I repotted it. Did I kill it?

Almost certainly not - a few weeks of sulking after repotting is completely normal, and some leaf loss or limp traps is part of the deal. The plant has lost fine root hairs and needs time to rebuild them before it can support its foliage. Keep it damp with distilled water, give it bright but not scorching light, and leave it alone rather than fiddling. Judge recovery by whether new growth appears from the centre, not by the state of the old leaves.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
A plant arrived in the post bare root and looks half dead. What do I do?

Pot it immediately rather than leaving it in the packaging - fresh 1:1 peat and perlite for most species, airy sphagnum and bark for Nepenthes. Spread the roots gently in the pot, settle it at the depth it was clearly growing before, and water it thoroughly with distilled water. Keep it somewhere bright but out of scorching direct sun for the first week, and raise the humidity a little if it is a Nepenthes or a sundew. Limpness and some leaf loss after shipping is normal, so give it a few weeks and watch for new growth from the centre.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Should I trim the leaves off a bare root plant when it arrives?

Leave anything green alone - even a tired leaf still feeds the plant while it re-roots. Trim only what is clearly dead, black or mushy, using clean scissors so you do not leave rotting tissue against the crown. Pot it straight away in fresh nutrient-free mix, water with distilled water, and keep it in bright but not scorching light for the first week. Some leaf loss over the following weeks is a normal part of settling in.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Is it better to divide in winter while the plant is asleep or in summer?

For temperate species the sweet spot is early spring, at the very end of dormancy - the plant is still dormant enough that disturbance costs little, but it has a full growing season ahead to re-root. Dividing deep in winter is workable for Sarracenia but the pieces sit there doing nothing for months and are more prone to rot. Dividing in summer means cutting into a plant that is actively supporting a lot of foliage, so it sulks badly. Nepenthes and other tropicals have no dormancy and are separated whenever they are growing well.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What should I do with the little offsets my Sarracenia keeps making?

You can leave them and let the plant build into an impressive clump, or separate them at repotting time in early spring. If you separate, make sure each offset comes away with roots of its own and at least one growth point, then pot it in fresh peat and sand. Small divisions often skip pitchering for a season while they establish, which is normal. Spares make excellent trades or gifts once they have settled in.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do I know if a division is big enough to survive on its own?

It needs two things: its own roots and at least one clear growth point or crown. A chunk of rhizome with a growth point but no roots can sometimes be coaxed along in damp sphagnum, but it is slow and risky. A generous division with plenty of root establishes far faster than a sliver, so resist the temptation to cut a plant into as many pieces as physically possible. Bigger pieces will often pitcher or trap the same season, while tiny ones spend a year just rebuilding.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Whats the deal with tissue culture - can I do that at home?

Tissue culture grows plants from tiny pieces of sterile tissue on a nutrient gel in sealed vessels, and it is how nurseries produce thousands of identical flytraps cheaply. It demands genuine sterile technique - a still air box or flow hood, sterilised tools and media, and everything sealed against contamination - because a single mould spore ruins a flask. Hobbyists do run it at home successfully, but it is a serious project with real equipment costs, not a casual afternoon. For most growers, leaf pullings and divisions get you more plants with far less trouble.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Do I need to sterilise anything when I take cuttings normally?

For ordinary propagation on open media you do not need lab sterility, but basic hygiene pays off. Wipe your blade or scissors with isopropyl alcohol between plants so you are not moving rot or pests around, use fresh mix rather than reused peat, and use distilled or rainwater rather than tap. Since cuttings sit under high humidity where fungus thrives, cleanliness matters more than usual. Full sterile technique with a still air box only comes into play for tissue culture.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How should I pack a plant if I'm posting one to someone?

Send it bare root: rinse the media off, wrap the roots in damp sphagnum or damp paper towel, then bag the root zone and tape it so moisture stays put and the foliage stays dry. Wrap the whole plant in a bit of newspaper or bubble to stop it rattling, box it snugly, and post early in the week so it does not sit in a depot over the weekend. Avoid extreme weather - a plant frozen or cooked in transit rarely recovers. Tell the recipient to pot it up straight away and expect a few weeks of limpness.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Are there any rules about swapping plants with other growers?

Trading is how most collections grow and it is the best way to get unusual clones cheaply, but check the rules before anything crosses a border - many carnivorous plants are covered by CITES and international shipping needs paperwork. Within your own country, swapping divisions and pullings is generally straightforward. Send healthy pest-free material only, label everything with the full name and clone if it has one, and be honest about the size of what you are sending. Keep new arrivals separate from your collection for a few weeks so you do not import pests.
